title: The Joy of the Dwelling and the Unity of the Inhabitants
english: Guarding the rights of God by uncircumcised memory (Ps 118:162).

The word has its own meaning for David, that being pursued by Saul in vain and through envy, he ceased to resist through fear toward God; and it extends to the common experience, that of the wars of rulers there is no other way to be escaped from being harmed than by being guarded by the fear of God. After the gift of wisdom, he asks again for salvation from dangers (Ps 118:173); this too is a reward for the voluntary zeal concerning the divine law (Ps 118:174-175).

Thus, he was saying that he expected eternal salvation, and now he observes that this study of the law is being performed with longing. For he says that he will indeed seek and praise God through His all-wise judgments, having been helped by this, which is Christ, descending in place of men to death for the salvation of men, and being driven out to suffer, redeeming those in sufferings and those dying through death; following which, the 'My soul shall live' and the following verses follow (Ps 119:2).

This was indeed immediately after the first apostasy of man when Cain struck down his brother by deceit, but it is also through the whole age of the present, as is shown in other things and in this present matter. Therefore, the man who turns toward God, suffering and being afflicted, asks for salvation from Him. He does not foresee the scarcity lying then, when he shall be brought up to the dwelling of the city of peace and the citizenship with both the good and the bad (Ps 119:5).

Another also makes manifest the foreign land from one part, into which Israel, having fallen, dwelt, and indeed his sojourning to extend for the longest time. Prophesying in lamentation, he brings this forth as reaching even to the present established state; for this is the longest (Ps 119:7).

For the good and God-fearing ones make their own peace and with all men, when they do not lack the critical punishment which God had commanded against the Canaanites and Amorites, forbidding friendship toward them; but the wicked and those ignoring God would never come into friendship with the good, but they loathe godliness and do not favorably receive even the good things from the God-fearing, nor are they moved by the philanthropy of them (Ps 120:1b). Mountains, say...
There are the unsetting and heavenly powers there; and while waiting for help through these, he says that help does not spring from these, but from the Creator.

Regarding Ps 121:1b, joy is to hear what is said by the angels, namely those speaking to the prophets, such as the flocks beginning the Israelite [process], which is he who is shown through Zechariah, both acting as an ambassador on behalf of the fallen Jerusalem and speaking of its coming habitation. This is indeed what the singer says he heard and was made glad by, having foreseen the stable habitation in the holy city, perceiving it prophetically as the matter is present. For this is the 'Our feet have been standing in the courts of Jerusalem' (Ps 122:2). But the standing of feet is an immovable habitation, which even the holy prophets proclaim, whereas the opposite was when, according to history, God shook the foot of Jerusalem from its inhabited land. Therefore the singer speaks of the desolation of the city, having seen it just as Ezekiel did, but of the building up as a city being united, not according to the usual way, namely by surrounding it with walls, but by the inhabitants being united to one another. Therefore also he has not said 'a city', but as a city having a togetherness together. For neither does Ezekiel foretell that it shall be inhabited by walls, nor does Zechariah, but without walls; rather its wall shall be the Lord, because God is the guardian and companion of the unity of the saints. He interprets then the being through them of the inhabitants as the union, saying, 'There the tribes ascended, tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel to confess in the name of the Lord' (Ps 122:4). Not that they surrounded walls, and because of this they were united, but that they were united through themselves. A testimony indeed to Israel, namely testifying the truth of the promises, but to confess in the name of the Lord, meaning that to him who fulfilled the wonderful promise, a confession of graces is owed by those being benefited. He says that thrones of the house of David were established upon it, since even a kingdom is prophesied by Daniel, not only a principality of someone or the rule of one, but a common rule for the best and most God-fearing, through whom the kingdom of David is restored by the grace of Christ, who gave to the twelve apostles the right to judge, sitting upon the twelve thrones.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Commentary on Psalms
english: Israel. Regarding Psalm 124:3, evil people will not be allowed to destroy the good subjects, but after the good have suffered a little from them, He will free them from harmful slavery, which will not dare to fall upon those beginning under God. Regarding Psalm 126:1-2, Solomon is inscribed to the song because he built the temple. But he signifies the true Solomon, our Lord, the cause of the true and peaceful building. Therefore, this building is also shown to be god-made, and the firm guard in guarding according to God; and this is fitting, since the buildings, guards, and night-watches through men were passing into vainness, and the daytime care and toil. Therefore, such human things came forward so that the divine alone might be known to possess the firm and unchangeable, just as justice came through law so that God's justice might be shown with it, having the genuine and the only true, and true life after that which is in shadow and in image. When He gives sleep to His beloved, He has revealed the rest from God, resembling sleep, which will be given out of love.

Regarding Psalm 126:4a, 'Indeed, You have made me,' he says, 'Judah, as a bow to myself.' And here he speaks of the arrows of the Mighty toward the remaining saints against those lower than the ungodly and with injustice violent.

Regarding Psalm 127:1, many and various are the ways of entrance, and many-sided are the lives of those beginning, but one is the perfection reaching the summit. He characterizes those fearing the Lord, whoever they are, having said thus: 'Those walking in His ways.' For those not doing this do not fear the Lord. For the fear of the Lord is a turning away from evils, but he who is turned away from evils is ready for the divine ways.

Regarding Psalm 129:1b-2, it is possible for that from the depth, like waters, of the poured-out afflictions, but the endurance and the repetition of the same, being surpassed and being exhausted, and not willing to lift up the supplication because of desire. Therefore, 'Hear my voice and let your ears be attentive.' Regarding Psalm 131:6, to David, who had not foreseen, the place became manifest from the matter itself.

Therefore, 'We have heard and found,' he says, that God showed the threshing floor to Ornathan, upon which the altar was built to prevent the decaying death of the Hebrew race (Ps 131:8). Having loved the discovery as having known that which was desired of old, he rejoices in the thing and loves the worship there. It is there that he says God's presence occurs, because the glory of God became manifest through the presence of the angel.

Similarly, he says, he foretells the time concerning Solomon (Ps 131:9), in which the ark is moved from the tent and is established in the temple, and a divine glory shone and a cloud covered the house. These things, he says, we see to have happened to Solomon according to the words of David (Ps 131:10). For the favor is toward David (Ps 131:10). Even if the blessing is toward those after him, just as it is said in opposition to Solomon, that because of David all his kingship shall not fall, and indeed it has passed even to the descendants because of David's mercy, just as it is said concerning Hezekiah, 'I am a shield for this city because of David my servant' (2 Kings 22:20).

To the former and briefer gifts, it brings the greatest, being a preservation of all those (Ps 132:15). For he gave abundance of food from the beginning, which is called Thiran, though another interprets it as grain. And he promises to make the inhabitants satisfied, and he has made the counsel of priests and holy ones to be saved and to preside with the holy hymns. But of all these, having already been corrupted, and the nation being unable to enjoy even the good things of the earth because of the Roman authority, with the priesthood falling away and all the joy in the temple being dissolved, the great power—the horn of David, which has the power to gore all enemies, a fitting lamp shining with heavenly light for David and for his race, who, having begun at once upon all the world, sends out the torch, just as the prophet Simeon says, 'A light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for your people Israel' (Luke 2:32).

And the parable was of a divine matter, and that of the ointment; but the one from God is more prominent, according to the parable of the dew falling from heaven upon the mountains. For the gift and the good thing are heavenly, not human, nor appearing among men apart from the gift from above.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Likeness of God and the Stewardship of the Land
english: The work of hymns signifies the gathering of all saints (Ps 133:1-2), neither by day nor by night, as sleep does not overcome them by the power of those then incorruptible and tireless bodies.

Hymns are the end of good things, while the works of God are the hypothesis of hymns, being gifts and benefits (Ps 134:1-2). Those who hymn are not strangers or those standing far off, but those present and remaining, just as David established the hymn-singers as those staying upon this.

If anyone says that the indwelling of humans by God is a great benefit and the capital of all benefits (Ps 134:3-4), just as He made the Hebrews His own people and a chosen people for Himself above all nations then, setting them apart as something more and surpassing, as also He is His own God in intimacy, the God of all in creation.

He recalls the things happening paradoxically concerning Israel (Ps 134:6-7)—not things that would appear by nature from the beginning, but by the will of the One above nature (this indeed of the heavens, such as fire, hail, and darkness; this of the earth, such as frogs, locusts, gnats, and the punishing energy against the firstborn; and this of those in the sea and the depths, such as those concerning the Red Sea)—to the creative power, linking these as having come from the same power, asserting that He alone is the one moving the clouds from the ends of the earth, kindling lightning, sending the precursors of rains, and sending winds from the invisible beginning; He says that the generation of winds is an unseen and unknown treasure of God, not known beforehand where they are before they blow; he continuously understands that the winds lie as in the bodies, having treasures.

The terrible things signify not only what happened for Israel's sake, but for the knowledge of God through all the earth and all time (Ps 134:13), not only while the works of the one doing them were being made known, but also later through memory.

Therefore, he names those above as gods according to the custom of the nations, though they are not gods; but now, to the shame of the false gods' idols, he names them by the matter, accusing that silver...

And it is like gold, purified by labor, because it is like that which is under men and the soulless, along with the vanity of souls, due to the absence of a life-giving spirit upon them; all such things possess the outward appearance of contempt, and the demons have the outward indictment that they are not gods, whose such likenesses exist. For the likeness of God is divine; therefore also man is the icon of the divine, not one sustained by divinity.

Not less than subduing the warring ones, to feed them in the wilderness and to lead them without supplies, and the cutting down of the Amorite kings, is a demonstration of the mercy of God, providing a place for habitation, giving to the Hebrews their land (Ps 135:16, 22). And this was the storing up of the wealth of the ungodly for the righteous. For they would not have been destroyed otherwise if they had not been coming to the fullness of sins, just as God said to Abraham; and Moses indeed says that he has not held Israel in possession of their land because of his own righteousness, but because of their lawlessness and through the love of God toward the fathers, so that toward them indeed the destructive judgment was to be just, but toward these a philanthropic beneficent giving, and for the participation in philanthropy, the piety of the fathers had become a preparation. For thus justly and goodly and fittingly into order things from God appear.

That they are lying in the wilderness shows just as the state of the captives is after the migration from their own cities (Ps 136:1, 2). For this is: 'At the willow trees we hung up our instruments' (Ps 136:2).

And according to the spiritual worship, they considered foreign lands to be the foreign souls, and to be kept in these, to bring forth the divine things, just as being migrated from one's own place into a foreign place, as the divine mouth of Christ says: 'Do not give the holy things to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the swine' (Matt 7:6). Such was also Herod, desiring to behold the signs of Christ, not seeking this for reverence but for pleasant spectacle, wherefore he did not succeed.

'I will not use another land like yours, O Jerusalem,' he says, 'nor will I place on an equal the unclean with the pure, nor the profane near the holy; but for me, even being outside your habitation, your [one] will approach' (Ps 136:4, 5).
